tier_reason: Stays C (first-party). Enricher located the spdlog harness on the benchmark branch: async in-memory co/log vs synchronous spdlog basic_logger_mt, Linux rows under WSL, so the 13-24x headline is a harness artifact; caveats corrected.

corrections.caveats: First-party numbers; the spdlog harness lives on the separate `benchmark` branch (benchmark/log_bm.cc, linked only from readme_cn.md). It times co/log's asynchronous in-memory path against spdlog 1.8.5 basic_logger_mt, a synchronous mutex file sink (not spdlog's async logger), and the Linux rows ran under WSL per benchmark/readme.md (spdlog 2.08 s on WSL vs 0.46 s native Windows), so the 13-24x over spdlog is mostly WSL file I/O plus async-vs-sync. Numbers predate the current API (old LOG<< / log::exit), the Windows row differs between the two READMEs, no glog harness exists anywhere, and json_bm.cc also times simdjson but the README omits those rows. co/log is lossy under overload (drops the oldest half of its buffer past max_log_buffer_size 32 MB; the benchmark never counts written lines), the logger thread starts only from the flag::parse hook, timestamps lag up to 128 ms, and it installs process-wide signal handlers. Also publishes co/json vs rapidjson (1.4-3.6x) with the same tier-C caveats.

tier_reason: Stays C (first-party speed.html and the author's ICCAE 2025 paper). Enricher caveat correction: the paper's near-100% rows are compiler artifacts (sub-nanosecond timings flat in n), so only the speed.html expression-rewriting wins over IT++ and Newmat stand.

corrections.caveats: First-party numbers from a Core2 Duo (2 GHz) / Linux 2.6.26 / GCC 4.3.0 setup from Armadillo's early releases; flags and exact CPU model unstated, only a timing-loop extract shown, results are graphs with 'approximate speed-up' labels, and the baselines are IT++ and Newmat, not BLAS or Eigen. The wins come from expression rewriting rather than kernels (the 2.5x chain over IT++ matches a 2.63x multiply-add cut from reordering; the 1086x is consistent with a dense O(n^3) inverse in the baseline); Armadillo links BLAS/LAPACK for heavy kernels. The repo's ICCAE 2025 paper (Fig. 1) times 'optimised' trace(A*B) at 5.98e-11 to 2.71e-10 s and a'*diagmat(B)*c at 7.21e-10 to 8.54e-10 s, flat from n=100 to 1000 (under about 3 cycles for n^2 or n multiply-adds), so the compiler hoisted or dropped the fused inline trace and the 99.96-99.99% rows are timing artifacts; no harness for either page is in the repo. Issue #275 (tiny inv(A)*B slowdown in 11.0-14.4.1), #260/#285 (multi-thread small-matrix slowdowns); bounds checks and zero-fill are on by default.

tier_reason: Stays A (public ParserBench.cpp, MSVC 1913 flags in msvc2017.vcxproj, Xeon E5-2687W). Enricher caveat correction: the harness uses ExprTk as its own correctness oracle, and the per-expression lead is 3.4x median vs muparser 2.2.4, not 1.18x.

corrections.caveats: First-party suite (src/ParserBench.cpp, 32-bit MSVC 1913 runs only, logs stop in 2018): the score is a mean of time ratios inflated by constant-folded expressions; recounting the 2018 logs gives a per-expression median of 3.4x vs muparser 2.2.4 on bench_expr.txt (range 1.05-15.8x), 1.5x on random_with_functions and 4.1x on bench_expr_complete, with the best double rival (METL/FParser) at 1.2-2.5x. The harness hard-wires ExprTk as the correctness reference, so rivals that disagree are disqualified while ExprTk never can be, and ExprTk gets an extra untimed pass (double rivals barely affected; float builds, ExprTkFloat included, lose rows). muparserSSE (AsmJit JIT, float) won bench_expr_complete on points and was faster on 5,580 of the 6,198 expressions it passed. Bundled baselines are old (muparser 2.2.4). Last commit 2025-01-01.

tier_reason: Stays C (first-party DESIGN.md prose, CI-log numbers only). Enricher caveat correction: incomplete integer overflow check in the scanning hot path (inputs in the benchmark are in range, so the rows stand) and mislabelled harness rows.

corrections.caveats: One prose claim in DESIGN.md (scanning about 2x faster than sscanf) with no compiler, flags or CPU; the numbers exist only in CI logs (Debug and Release both run; the gcc-14/clang-19 matrix jobs have no install step, so they build with the runner's default compiler). bench_scan.cpp labels its sscanf rows 'snprintf' and its 'scan nothing' row times one memcmp against sscanf's whitespace-skipping format interpretation. Correctness: the overflow check in detail::parse_int (include/emio/reader.hpp) rejects only when value*base+digit wraps below the previous value, so '5000000000' scans into uint32_t as 705032704, '30000000000000000000' into uint64_t as 11553255926290448384 and hex '1FFFFFFFFFFFFFFFF' as 0xFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFF (about 75% of 10-digit values above UINT32_MAX accepted; signed paths hit overflow UB; unit tests try only max+1 and max*10); benchmark inputs are in range, so the measured rows are unchanged. No float scanning; formatting (Dragon4) is self-reported 1.5-2x slower than fmt.

tier_reason: Stays C (first-party llvm-mca estimates). Enricher caveat correction: the GLM motor row computes a different quantity (R^T p without translation, normalizing every call), so the motor gap is not like-for-like.

corrections.caveats: Evidence is llvm-mca static cycle estimates (Skylake model), not measured run time, from docs/perf.md. The GLM baseline is scalar (0.9.9.7, no GLM_FORCE_INTRINSICS; its SIMD quaternion multiply is commented out, so the rotor row is representative). The GLM motor row (5435 vs 1831 cycles) computes glm::mat3x4_cast(a) * b with a vec4 b that GLM silently converts to vec3, yielding R^T p with no translation (the correct call is b * mat3x4_cast(a)), and the GLM routine normalizes on every call while Klein's m(p) assumes a normalized motor, so the ~3x motor gap compares different computations; the listing also loads only 3 floats of the point. Ties RTM; the RTM qvv routine in perf/rtm_perf.cpp has no published result. Normalize uses approximate rcp/rsqrt (about 22 bits); open bug #30 (gpLL e23/e12 swap, patch never merged). No independent run-time benchmark (ga-benchmark excludes Klein). Archived 2024-08-02.

tier_reason: Stays C (first-party). The NumKong README (re-found by w1-mine-e, recorded as a duplicate id) adds library comparison tables, folded into the caveats here.

corrections.caveats: Baseline is GCC-12 auto-vectorized scalar C loops (built with -ffast-math per the author's blog), not a literal std:: facility call. Exact CPU SKU not given (Intel Sapphire Rapids, single-threaded), and the README table does not name the benchmark code, so tier stays C. The 118x JS-divergence figure matches the blog's 118.84x (avx512_f16 vs serial_f16 at 1536d, where the serial baseline calls libc logf). The repo was renamed from SimSIMD to NumKong (github.com/ashvardanian/SimSIMD redirects). The NumKong README also publishes first-party library tables (NumPy 2.4 + OpenBLAS, PyTorch 2.10 + MKL, JAX 0.9): dot product 2048-d f32 7.1 gso/s vs NumPy 1.5, PyTorch 0.6 and JAX 0.4; f64 5.8 vs 2.0; f16 11.5 vs NumPy 0.2 and PyTorch 0.5; i8 14.8 vs NumPy 1.1 (overflowing); matmul 2048x2048 i8 1279 gso/s vs PyTorch+MKL 50.0 and e5m2 398 vs 0.4, but it is slower on f64 (8.6 vs 65.5 NumPy+OpenBLAS and 68.2 PyTorch+MKL), f32 (37.7 vs 140 and 145) and bf16 (458 vs 851 PyTorch); no flags and no exact CPU model for those tables either.

tier_reason: Stays C (third-party single-run Ruby bench, vendor site blocked). Enricher caveat correction: rank 10th of 37 on time and second on 8-thread RSS, not the highest RSS.

corrections.caveats: Third-party SamSaffron/allocator_bench (Ruby, GVL-serialised threads, single runs, no CPU or compiler): 1.15-1.48x vs glibc but 10th of 37 on time (tcmalloc 2.0-2.7, rpmalloc and jemalloc 5.2.0 faster) and second-highest 8-thread RSS of 37 (rpmalloc master higher). The 'mem' column is end-of-run RSS from ps, not peak; retained sizes use an unseeded Random.rand so the workload differs per run; tcmalloc 2.1 vs 2.2 differ by 14.5% at 1 thread, the same size as lockless's margin. The bench preloaded libllalloc.so.1.4 while the jl2922/lockless_allocator mirror (2017, 0 stars) builds .so.1.3. x86-only assembly, real sbrk slabs, mallopt/malloc_trim ignore their parameters, a fork child leaks other threads' heaps. Vendor numbers (locklessinc.com, blocked) and Percona 2012 (best throughput group, mysqld RSS +5 GB) seen as snippets only. GPL-3.0-or-later; code copyright 2009-2011, last update July 2012, abandoned.

tier_reason: Stays C (first-party Python charts). Enricher caveat correction: the chart-era run preprocessed RapidFuzz inputs once but FuzzyWuzzy inside the timed loop, the cdist bars are the narrowest-lane batched path, and the current script no longer runs.

corrections.caveats: First-party charts (scorer.svg 2021-09-10, cdist.svg 2022-10-02) from RapidFuzz's Python bench scripts, single runs, no compiler, flags or CPU: the Python wrapper is timed against FuzzyWuzzy called from Python, not C++ against C++. The chart-era script (69fc902) ran default_process once per string for RapidFuzz but FuzzyWuzzy's full_process inside all 1,000,000 timed calls; whether FuzzyWuzzy had the python-Levenshtein speedup is unstated. The cdist chart pits one batched single-threaded cdist call against a Python double loop on length-8 strings (the narrowest SIMD lane width; 32 queries per AVX2 batch), and only ratio, token_sort_ratio and QRatio have the batched Multi* path, which are the biggest bars (258x, 717x, 622x), so the gap is mostly removed interpreter overhead plus batching. Neither chart reproduces now: commit 6925381 passes processor=True (TypeError on 6 of 8 scorers since RapidFuzz 3.0) and requirements.txt lists thefuzz, which is built on rapidfuzz. Both charts predate the 1.10.2 partial_ratio equal-length symmetry fix (current code runs a second reversed pass, up to 2x the measured work) and the cdist chart ran SIMD code added the same day, before its UB and SSE2 fixes. The C++ library has no extract/cdist/default_process and no NEON; extras/rapidfuzz_amalgamated.hpp is stale (v1.0.2 banner, WRatio len_ratio bug fixed in 3.3.3). StringZilla's README reports 15,680 vs 4,970 MCUPS over rapidfuzz cdist on about 100-byte DNA Levenshtein (one core, Xeon 4).

tier_reason: Stays C (first-party single run). Enricher caveat correction: the README numbers measure 2014 code with a different quick sort; comparator truncation hazard.

corrections.caveats: One 10,000-element lrand48 int64 run on a 2014 MacBook Pro with compiler and flags unstated, qsort called through a function pointer (macOS libc), not compared against std::sort. The table is unchanged since commit 47934fc (2014-05-04) and timed the old middle-pivot quick sort with no depth limit (the issue #62 stack-overflow version); the shipping 2019 median-of-5/heap-fallback/sorting-network quick sort has never been re-benchmarked. Comparator results are stored in an int (partition, binary insertion find, in-place merge), so the README's own ((x) - (y)) int64 example truncates differences wider than 32 bits (with more than 16 multiples of 2^32 the all-equal shortcut leaves the range unsorted) and double keys with a subtraction comparator truncate differences below 1.0 to 0; the MEDIAN else branch compares dst[a] with dst[b] instead of dst[c] (pivot quality only, open PR #84); the stress test returns 0 on FAILED; demo and benchmark override SORT_CSWAP with branchless MIN/MAX; tim sort exits on OOM.

tier_reason: Stays A (public harness, gcc 16.1.1 -O3, Ryzen 9 7950X). Enricher caveat correction: the headline inline-build win is against an unreserved std::vector.

corrections.caveats: Own harness (test/bench/solo.cpp, gcc 16.1.1 -O3, Ryzen 9 7950X): wins only inline-storage and string work. The headline 3.1x build-7-inline row is against a std::vector that is never reserved (it starts empty and reallocates at 1/2/4/8, 4 mallocs per vector; no reserve(7) baseline is measured), and the 12% shuffle+sort lead runs std::sort on raw storage, so the container design does not explain it; the two bolded wins (emplace_back string 3.9%, insert-front string 6.7%) sit inside the stated ~7% noise. Slower than std::vector on push_back (2.2x), subscript (18%) and swap. v1.0.x had data-corruption bugs fixed in v1.1.0 (2026-07-28): push_back(v[0]) segfault #50, erase(it,it) and empty-range insert blanking elements #65/#66, double destroy #68; Conan Center still lists only 1.0.2 and 1.0.3. The 1-byte overhead holds only for 1-byte T (8 bytes when alignof(T) is 8).

tier_reason: Downgraded C to D: the only faster rows (virtual_ptr 0.18-0.22x) come from a harness in which virtual_ptr copies prebuilt fat pointers from a contiguous vector into empty overriders that never read the object while the virtual-function row dereferences random heap objects, so the win is a cache-layout artifact (AssemblyScript and Blosc precedent); ordinary dispatch is 1.09-2.47x slower than virtual functions.

corrections.caveats: Project's own tests/benchmarks.cpp (Google Benchmark, no CPU model): ordinary open-method dispatch is 1.09-2.47x slower than virtual functions. The only faster rows (virtual_ptr 0.18-0.22x) copy prebuilt fat pointers from a contiguous vector and call empty overriders that never read the object, while the virtual-function row loads the vptr from one of 100,000 random heap objects and pays the cache miss; with a virtual base, where the object must be touched, virtual_ptr turns 2.1x slower. avg is the Google Benchmark mean minus a no-dispatch baseline (dev/bmutils.py); the odd cache sizes are byte counts printed as KiB; alloc_dist is declared but never used. Issue #36 (duplicate overrider crashes at call time). Archived 2026-03-04, superseded by Boost.OpenMethod (Boost 1.90), whose docs claim no speed-up over virtual functions. No spec category fits; filed with the fat-pointer and delegate libraries under smart-pointers-and-refcount.

corrections.caveats: Medal table ranks by CPU time on WSL1 (15.625 ms tick) while each repetition runs 20-200 us, so 89-93% of cases read 0.0 and golds are ties; wall-clock data shows Versor fourth behind GATL, Gaalet and Gaalop. tier_reason: Tier C stays: both harnesses are public in the repo (ccan/htable/tools/speed.c and ccan/jmap/tools/speed.c), but the 2010 blog numbers name no CPU, compiler or libJudy version and predate the 2022 bit-stealing fix and the density change.

tier_reason: First-party benchmark stays tier C; its nlohmann baseline is handicapped (DOM rebuilt per call, vector grown from empty and copied, no sax_parse) while BitSerializer reuses pre-reserved buffers.

tier_reason: Tier A stays (public harness, gcc 8.3.0, flags per row, i7-4510U), with the mixed-run headline and harness tilt recorded.

corrections.caveats: Headline mixes a September 2019 -O3 run for Google protobuf 3.6.1 and protobuf-c with a January 2020 -O2 rerun of pbtools only (commit 6000b5f). Security: packed fixed-width repeated fields with a payload length not a multiple of the element size write past the arena allocation (read in lib/src/pbtools.c, untested). N-byte encode buffer holds N-1 bytes; NUL-terminated strings; proto3 only; abandoned since 2023-06-04.

tier_reason: Tier C stays; first-party timing with an unoptimised driver and open decoder out-of-bounds reads.

Unmaintained since 2015; Python 2 model generator; default model lacks digits and spaces.

tier_reason: Tier C stays; both benchmark sources link a prebuilt distro protobuf-c runtime against a from-source nanopb, so the flag labels do not describe the measured runtime, though the direction holds at 4.7x encode and 2.4x decode (derived).

tier_reason: The 2001 cycle counts come from a harness whose glibc call pays first-call sysconf and malloc costs while dietlibc gets the warm path, and the measured dietlibc qsort and bsearch had correctness bugs (quadratic on equal keys; bsearch reads past the array end and misses present keys) that were fixed later, so the numbers describe neither the current code nor a fair comparison (bug-in-measured-path precedent). Directional only.

corrections.caveats: 2001 changelog cycle counts (qsort 300010 vs 679414, bsearch 553 vs 3352) from harness t.c (commit 344deb2): one rdtsc call each, glibc's timed call pays sysconf(_SC_PHYS_PAGES) and malloc on first use, bsearch unwarmed. Measured qsort went quadratic on equal keys and measured bsearch read past the array end (fixed 0.10-0.15); qsort rewritten 2003, 2006, 2012 (rand pivot) and 2019. HEAD qsort makes about 1.8x more comparisons than glibc's merge sort on random keys. Mirror archived; upstream last commit 2019-03-18; GPL-2.0-or-later.

tier_reason: Tier C stays; the PR #53 harness neither protects the encode output from elimination nor checks decode results, and the headline is unsafe_mode.
